title: The Valuation Gap: Why the Number in Your Head Rarely Matches the Number on Paper
linkedin:
Most owners can tell you what their business is worth in about two seconds. Ask where the number came from, and it gets a lot less precise.

A figure that feels proportionate to the years put in. A rough multiple mentioned by a peer at a barbecue. What the next chapter of life would actually need. All perfectly human ways to land on a number. None of them is how a buyer, a bank or a formal valuation actually prices a business.

A proper valuation triangulates instead of guessing. It runs the business through an EBITDA multiple benchmarked against real comparable transactions, a discounted cash flow view of future earnings, and an asset based floor check. When those three land close together, the number carries weight. When they diverge sharply, the gap itself is the useful part, usually pointing straight at customer concentration, owner dependence or a thin management layer.

The owners who handle this well aren't the ones with the highest number. They're the ones who found out what the real number was early enough to do something about the gap. A valuation commissioned two years out from a decision is a planning document. The same exercise commissioned two months out, once a sale or a family transition has forced the question, is closer to an autopsy.

The business hasn't changed between those two moments. The owner's options have.

Quick one for any business owner who has ever said "I reckon it's worth about..." when someone asks what their business is worth.

That number is almost always built from effort, not from what a buyer would actually pay. A real valuation looks at future earnings, risk and comparable sales, not years put in or a mate's rough guess.

The gap between the two numbers usually isn't random either. It tends to point at something specific, like too much revenue sitting with one or two customers, or too much of the business living in the owner's head.

Genuinely curious: if you had to guess your business's value right now, how confident are you that a formal valuation would land anywhere close?

A note for business owners across Brisbane, Queensland, New South Wales and Victoria who have ever wondered what their business is actually worth.

Most owners carry a number in their head, usually built from the years they have put in, a figure a peer mentioned once, or a rough multiple of revenue picked up somewhere along the way. It is a completely understandable way to arrive at a figure. It is also rarely the number a formal valuation produces.

A proper valuation looks at the business differently. It typically runs three methods at once, an earnings multiple benchmarked against comparable sales, a forecast of future cash flow, and an asset based floor value, then checks where they agree and where they do not. The businesses that manage this best are not the ones with the highest number. They are the ones who found out what the real number was early enough to do something useful with it, whether that means reducing reliance on a handful of customers or tidying up the systems that currently only exist in the owner's head.

Two years out from any decision, that number is a planning tool. Two months out, once a sale or a transition has already forced the question, it is closer to a surprise.

Read the full piece on the blog for a plain look at how the three valuation methods actually work and why they can land in different places on the same set of numbers.
